title: SARAH CALLED ABRAHAM “LORD”—Why Did Peter Bring That Into a Teaching About Marriage?
paragraphs: SARAH CALLED ABRAHAM “LORD”—Why Did Peter Bring That Into a Teaching About Marriage?

One word has been used to make women afraid, make men feel powerful, and turn a beautiful passage about fearless faith into something Peter never intended. But when you read what Sarah actually said—and then keep reading what Peter says to husbands—the passage becomes far more confronting to both men and women than most people realize.
There is a sentence in the New Testament that can make a modern reader stop cold.
“Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord.”
There it is.
1 Peter 3:6.
And depending on what kind of church you grew up in, what kind of marriage you witnessed, or what someone once told you “biblical submission” means, those words may sound beautiful...
or deeply uncomfortable.
Maybe somebody has even used this verse against you.
Maybe you have heard it preached as though Peter were saying, “A godly wife should treat her husband like a king.”
Maybe a husband has read it and quietly thought, “See? The Bible says I’m the boss.”
Maybe a wounded wife has read it and wondered whether following Jesus means losing her voice.
Or maybe you have simply skipped over it because you did not know what to do with it.
But there is something hiding in plain sight.
Something many readers never notice.
Peter did not invent Sarah’s words.
He reached backward roughly two thousand years before his own time and pulled a tiny sentence out of Sarah’s life.
And when you go back and find that sentence...
the scene is nothing like what you might expect.
Sarah was not kneeling before Abraham.
She was not standing before a congregation teaching women to address their husbands as “lord.”
Abraham had not commanded her to use an honorific.
In fact...
Sarah was laughing.
God had promised something so impossible that Sarah laughed inside herself.
She was old.
Abraham was old.
The promise of a son appeared biologically absurd.
And Genesis 18:12 records her inward response:
“After I am waxed old shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?”
The Hebrew expression translated “my lord” is:
אֲדֹנִי
ʾadoni.
“My lord.”
It can function as a respectful way of referring to a human superior or one held in honor. It does not make Abraham divine. It certainly does not place Abraham where only God belongs.
And notice something extraordinary.
Sarah apparently was not even saying this to Abraham.
She was speaking within herself.
That matters.
Because respect that exists only when someone is watching is performance.
Sarah’s words reveal something about the posture she carried toward Abraham even inside the privacy of her own thoughts.
Centuries later, Peter remembers her.
His Greek reads:
ὡς Σάρρα ὑπήκουσεν τῷ Ἀβραάμ, κύριον αὐτὸν καλοῦσα
hōs Sarra hypēkousen tō Abraam, kyrion auton kalousa
“as Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord...”
But stop.
Please do not build an entire theology of marriage from half a sentence.
Because Peter keeps writing.
And what comes next changes the emotional temperature of the passage.
He tells these women to do good...
and not be controlled by fear.
καὶ μὴ φοβούμεναι μηδεμίαν πτόησιν
and not fearing any terror/intimidation.
Read that again.
Peter speaks about submission...
and then speaks about fearlessness.
That should make us careful.
Biblical submission is not presented here as terrified compliance.
Peter does not tell Christian women to become frightened shadows of themselves.
He does not tell them that holiness means enduring every sinful demand without question.
He does not tell them their husband has become their god.
He points to holy women who “hoped in God.”
That is the center of gravity.
God.
Not Abraham.
Not the husband.
God.
The deepest security of the godly woman Peter describes does not come from having a perfect husband.
It comes from hoping in a perfect God.
And suddenly Sarah becomes painfully relatable.
Because Abraham was not a perfect husband.
Read Genesis carefully.
This marriage had scars.
There were moments of extraordinary faith.
There were also moments of fear.
There was displacement.
There was infertility.
There was waiting.
There was conflict.
There was Hagar.
There was heartbreak.
There were decisions Abraham made that exposed Sarah to danger.
There were years when the promise of God must have seemed almost cruel in its delay.
Sarah was not married to a flawless man.
Abraham was a man of tremendous faith who still had tremendous failures.
And Sarah was not a cardboard Bible character smiling serenely through every chapter.
She laughed at God's seemingly impossible promise.
She knew disappointment.
She knew what it was like to wait until her body appeared to have become evidence against what God had spoken.
Somebody reading this knows that feeling.
You prayed.
You waited.
You believed.
Then another year passed.
And another.
You watched other people receive what you begged God for.
Another marriage restored.
Another baby born.
Another prayer answered.
Another testimony posted online.
And you smiled for them while something inside you whispered:
“Lord... what about me?”
Sarah knew that room.
She knew the strange place where faith and disappointment can occupy the same heart.
And still...
God was writing.
That may be one of the reasons this passage is so powerful.
Peter does not point to Sarah because her life was painless.
He points to a woman whose hope ultimately had to reach beyond circumstances.
A woman living inside a story she could not yet see completed.
And perhaps that is where this passage finds you.
You do not know how your chapter ends yet.
You only know this chapter hurts.
But unfinished is not the same thing as abandoned.
Now something even more important happens.
Peter turns to husbands.
And men, we cannot suddenly close the Bible here.
The next verse begins with the same kind of relational seriousness.
Husbands are commanded to live with their wives “according to knowledge”—with understanding—and to give them honor.
Honor.
Not humiliation.
Not domination.
Not contempt.
Not spiritual intimidation.
Honor.
And then Peter says something breathtaking about husband and wife.
They are together heirs of the grace of life.
Grace has leveled the ground at the foot of the cross.
The Christian husband does not stand closer to salvation because he is male.
His wife is not spiritually second-class.
She is an heir of grace.
She belongs to Christ.
She bears God's image.
She is someone for whom Christ died.
And Peter gives husbands a warning that should make every Christian man examine how he treats his wife:
Your prayers can be hindered.
Think about the weight of that.
A man may sound spiritual in public.
He may know theology.
He may quote Scripture.
He may lead prayer.
He may raise his hands in worship.
He may post Bible verses.
He may be respected at church.
But Peter drags his Christianity through the front door of his house and asks:
How do you treat your wife?
Because heaven is not impressed by public spirituality that becomes cruelty behind closed doors.
You cannot use Scripture to crush the woman Peter commands you to honor and then imagine that quoting more Scripture makes you righteous.
You cannot demand Sarah while refusing to become a man who fears God.
You cannot demand respect while feeding contempt.
You cannot demand submission while refusing sacrificial love, understanding, repentance, gentleness, faithfulness, and honor.
And husbands should notice another detail.
Peter does not command the husband to make his wife submit.
He addresses the wife concerning her conduct...
then addresses the husband concerning his.
That means before using this passage as binoculars to inspect your spouse, use it as a mirror.
Wife...
what is Christ asking of you?
Husband...
what is Christ asking of you?
Because marriage becomes dangerous when Scripture is used primarily as ammunition against the other person.
“God says YOU have to...”
“You're supposed to...”
“The Bible says YOU...”
Meanwhile, nobody is trembling before what God said to them.
Maybe that is the word somebody's marriage needs tonight.
Put down the weaponized Bible verse.
Pick up the mirror.
The Gospel does not merely teach us how to identify someone else's sin.
It brings us face-to-face with our own.
And this is where we have to be especially careful with the word “lord.”
Sarah calling Abraham “lord” does not mean Abraham became her Lord in the ultimate sense.
There is only One before whom every Christian finally bows.
Jesus Christ.
The same New Testament that can use kyrios—“lord”—as a respectful designation for human beings uses it supremely of Jesus Christ.
A Christian marriage can have order.
It can have honor.
It can have submission.
It can have responsibility.
But it can never have two Saviors.
Husbands are not Jesus.
Wives are not Jesus.
Your spouse cannot carry the weight of being your Messiah.
And some marriages are suffocating because two broken human beings are asking each other to provide what only Christ can provide.
Perfect security.
Perfect validation.
Perfect fulfillment.
Perfect understanding.
Perfect love.
Your husband cannot save you.
Your wife cannot save you.
Jesus can.
And that is where this stops being merely an article about marriage.
Because perhaps your greatest problem tonight is not your spouse.
Perhaps your greatest problem is the same problem beneath every human scandal.
Sin.
Pride.
Fear.
Selfishness.
Control.
Resentment.
Lust.
Bitterness.
Unforgiveness.
The desperate desire to be lord of our own lives.
That is the scandal underneath all our scandals.
We want the throne.
And Jesus did not come merely to improve our relationships.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
The Son of God entered our brokenness.
He lived without sin.
He carried our guilt to the cross.
He was crucified.
He died.
And He rose again.
Grace does not pretend our sin is harmless.
Grace takes sin so seriously that Christ bore its judgment.
And grace loves sinners so deeply that Christ willingly came to save.
That changes marriage.
Because the Gospel creates a kind of person the world cannot manufacture.
A husband strong enough to repent.
A wife secure enough to hope in God.
A husband humble enough to say, “I was wrong.”
A wife free enough not to be ruled by fear.
Two sinners learning to forgive because they themselves have been forgiven.
Two wounded people refusing to make wounds their identity.
Two imperfect people kneeling before one perfect Lord.
Jesus.
Maybe you have been reading this whole article thinking about your husband.
Or your wife.
But what if the Holy Spirit has been putting His finger on you?
Not them.
You.
Your pride.
Your fear.
Your secret resentment.
Your controlling behavior.
Your coldness.
Your harsh words.
Your emotional withdrawal.
Your hidden sin.
Your refusal to apologize.
Your obsession with winning arguments.
Your habit of using Scripture to defend yourself instead of allowing Scripture to expose you.
Be honest.
Did this hit somewhere you were not expecting?
Conviction is not your enemy when it leads you to Christ.
Repentance is not humiliation.
It is the doorway home.
You do not have to protect the version of yourself Jesus is trying to transform.
You can confess.
You can repent.
You can ask forgiveness.
You can begin again.
Maybe your marriage has become a place where everybody is keeping score.
Who apologized last.
Who hurt whom more.
Who initiated affection.
Who failed first.
Who deserves what.
Then look at the cross.
Jesus did not save you because your score was impressive.
He saved by grace.
That does not erase justice, wisdom, healthy boundaries, or accountability.
It does mean Christians never graduate from needing mercy.
Sarah's story was not spotless.
Abraham's story was not spotless.
Peter's story certainly was not spotless.
Remember who wrote this letter.
Peter.
The man who swore he would never abandon Jesus...
and then denied Him three times.
Peter knew something about failure.
Peter knew something about fear.
Peter knew something about saying the wrong thing.
Peter knew something about collapsing under pressure.
But Peter also knew something else.
Restoration.
Jesus came looking for him.
Jesus restored him.
Jesus recommissioned him.
The man who once buckled under fear eventually wrote to believers about doing good without surrendering to fear.
That is grace.
God does not have to erase your history to redeem your future.
He can take the chapter you wish had never happened and make it the place where you finally learned how desperately you needed Christ.
That is the Gospel Warrior heartbeat.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by renaming sin.
Not by hiding wounds beneath Christian vocabulary.
Jesus rewrites lives through truth, repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and transforming grace.
So perhaps the real question is no longer:
“Why did Sarah call Abraham lord?”
Perhaps the deeper question is:
“Who is lord of me?”
Because you can win every argument about marriage and still lose your soul.
You can correctly parse the Greek and never surrender to the Christ who inspired Peter to write it.
You can know kyrios means “lord” while refusing to confess Jesus as Lord with your life.
You can defend biblical marriage publicly while destroying your marriage privately.
You can demand respect while refusing repentance.
You can appear Christian while your heart quietly belongs to yourself.
Jesus does not merely want better behavior decorating an unsurrendered heart.
He wants you.
All of you.
The hidden room.
The marriage nobody sees.
The resentment nobody knows about.
The browser history.
The private conversations.
The tears.
The pride.
The fear.
The wounds.
The excuses.
Bring them into the light.
There is grace there.
If this exposed something in you, do not turn the comment section into a courtroom for your spouse.
Make it an altar for your own heart.

And if you have watched Jesus restore something in your marriage that once looked impossible, tell your testimony. Somebody reading these comments may desperately need evidence that broken chapters do not always have to become final chapters.
Because one day, in the middle of an argument, disappointment, fear, or a season when your marriage feels painfully ordinary, you may need to remember:
Your spouse is not your Savior.
Jesus is.
It does not.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
It never could.
Supporting a ministry must never be manipulated into a spiritual tax.
But voluntary generosity can genuinely become an act of worship when it comes from a willing heart that desires to help Gospel truth reach more people.
Your support helps keep the mission moving.
But the greatest reason to support Gospel work is not merchandise.
It is people.
There is another Sarah somewhere.
Another Abraham.
Another Peter.
Another exhausted believer reading silently at 2:00 in the morning.
Another marriage barely holding together.
Another Christian hiding behind appearances.
Another skeptic wondering whether grace could possibly include them.
Another person one article away from opening a Bible again.
Another soul that needs to hear the name of Jesus.
That is why sharing matters.
That is why following matters.
That is why commenting matters.
That is why support matters.
whether you buy anything or never do...
do not miss the greater invitation.
Give Christ your heart.
Because eventually every marriage ends.
One day one spouse will bury the other, unless Christ returns first.
The photographs will fade.
The wedding clothes will disappear.
The house will belong to somebody else.
The arguments you thought you had to win will seem unbelievably small.
And husband and wife will each stand before God.
Not as somebody's spouse.
As a soul.
So love while you still have time.
Honor while you still have time.
Repent while you still have time.
Forgive while you still have time.
Say “I was wrong” while you still have time.
Pray together while you still have time.
Put Christ back in the center while you still have time.
Sarah called Abraham “lord.”
But Sarah and Abraham both needed the Lord.
So do we.
And maybe that is the sentence worth carrying with you long after this article disappears from your screen:
The safest marriage is not one where one sinner becomes lord over another—it is one where both finally realize they desperately need the same Lord.
